_note: A REFERENCE list of what is worth listening to near you, shown in the Tune panel. This file records nothing and creates no lanes -- it is the menu, not the meal. What the station actually records is bandplan.json. Keeping them separate is deliberate: a reference list should be wider than what you record, so you can see what you are choosing NOT to capture.
_measured_means: measured=true marks a frequency YOU have confirmed on YOUR receiver, with a real carrier in a sweep or real audio in a lane. Everything without it is taken from a published reference and is UNVERIFIED here. Do not set it because a frequency 'should' be active: a published allocation tells you what is licensed, not what is transmitting, and a peak-hold sweep overstates a burst. On the author's station six channels looked busy at +16 dB and produced zero audio in 317 recorded runs.
_encrypted_means: encrypted=true records that the traffic is unreadable even though the carrier is receivable. It is documentation, not a challenge. bandwatch makes no attempt to defeat encryption and no change that does will be accepted.

stations.name: GUARD — aviation distress
stations.note: International emergency. Silent until it is not.

stations.name: Tower (example)
stations.note: REPLACE with your local tower. Find it in your national aeronautical publication, then confirm with the air_survey lane.

stations.name: Ground (example)
stations.note: REPLACE with your local ground control.

stations.name: Approach (example)
stations.note: REPLACE. Approach often sits within 1.5 MHz of tower, which means one slice can hear both at once.

stations.name: MIL GUARD — distress
stations.note: The UHF twin of 121.5. Same frequency worldwide.

stations.name: UHF milair (example)
stations.note: REPLACE. Seed real frequencies from the milair_survey sweep — 225-400 MHz is 175 MHz of spectrum and guessing wastes a radio.

stations.name: VFIRE21 — fire mutual aid
stations.note: US national allocation. Still clear where it is used at all; most agencies have moved to 700/800 MHz.

stations.name: 700 MHz trunked (example)
stations.note: REPLACE with a control channel near you, found via the p25_survey sweep. Receivable is not readable — most modern systems are encrypted.

stations.name: FRS05
stations.note: Often the busiest of the block.

stations.name: MURS4
stations.note: 2.7 MHz from the 151 block — needs its own slice.

stations.name: NOAA WX7
stations.note: KNOWN-GOOD CONTROL. Transmits 24/7, so if the weather lane goes quiet the radio is broken, not the band.

stations.name: AAR 020 (example)
stations.note: US road channels run 159.81-161.565 in 15 kHz steps. Which ones are live is entirely local.

stations.name: ADS-B
stations.note: Aircraft position. A squawk of 7500/7600/7700 is a STRUCTURED emergency signal — it cannot be misheard, unlike a transcript.

stations.name: UAT
stations.note: The US general-aviation half of ADS-B. Invisible to a 1090-only receiver.

stations.name: ACARS
stations.note: Aircraft text, in the clear. No speech model involved, so no transcription error is possible.

stations.name: VDL2
stations.note: The newer aircraft datalink.

stations.name: APRS
stations.note: Ham position and telemetry (US). 144.80 in much of Europe.

stations.name: POCSAG/FLEX paging
stations.note: Dispatch traffic in PLAIN TEXT.

stations.name: TPMS
stations.note: Tyre sensors on passing vehicles. A TPMS id identifies a SENSOR, never a person — see docs/COVERAGE.md.

stations.name: ISM 433
stations.note: Weather stations, doorbells, remotes.

stations.name: ISM 915
stations.note: Utility smart meters (SCM+/ERT) in the US.

stations.name: FM band low
stations.note: KNOWN-GOOD CONTROL for the high-band radio. Carriers must always appear; if they do not, the problem is the receiver.
